blocks.text: Most DSA patterns you have studied so far are built around one core data structure: a heap, a trie, a segment tree, a Fenwick tree. You learn how that single structure works, and then you apply it across a family of problems that all lean on the same underlying trick.

Data Structure Design problems are different. The interviewer names a set of operations, for example insert, remove, and getRandom, and asks you to build a structure that supports all of them at a specific time complexity, usually O(1). No single structure from your toolbox does that on its own.

That is the entire point of this pattern group. You are not implementing a textbook structure from memory. You are combining two or more structures so that each one covers the gap the others leave behind.

items: LRU Cache: needs O(1) get, O(1) put, and O(1) eviction of the least recently used key
Insert Delete GetRandom O(1): needs O(1) insert, O(1) delete by value, and O(1) uniform random access
Min Stack: needs O(1) push, O(1) pop, and O(1) getMin at every point in time
Median Finder: needs to add numbers one at a time and return the running median faster than O(n) per query

blocks.text: In every one of these, a single hash map, array, heap, or linked list satisfies some of the requirements but not all of them at once. The skill this pattern group builds is recognizing which combination of already familiar structures satisfies every requirement at the same time.

You have already met every ingredient you need: hash maps, arrays, linked lists, stacks, heaps, and deques. This pattern group does not teach a new structure. It teaches you how to assemble the ones you already know into something none of them are alone.

Compare two prompts. Implement a trie tells you exactly which structure to build; the challenge is getting the mechanics right. Design a data structure that supports insert, delete, and getRandom, all in O(1) tells you nothing about which structure to use; the challenge is figuring that out yourself.

This second style of prompt is easy to recognize on LeetCode: the title usually starts with the word Design. LRU Cache, LFU Cache, Design Twitter, Design a data structure that supports insert, delete, and getRandom O(1), Find Median from Data Stream. Each one hands you a list of required operations instead of a structure name.

items: Every required operation comes with its own target time complexity, and all of them must hold at the same time, not just on average
The scenario is usually dressed up as something real, a cache, a social feed, a leaderboard, but underneath it is a pure data structure problem
No structure you learned as a standalone topic (array, hash map, heap, linked list, stack, tree) satisfies every required operation by itself
The interviewer is testing whether you can reason about trade offs across structures, not whether you memorized one structure implementation

blocks.text: This is also what separates Data Structure Design from an implementation question like implement a queue using two stacks. That question still names the target structure and asks you to rebuild it out of a different primitive. A design question gives you only behavior, and leaves the choice of structure entirely open.

The moment you see a problem statement listing several operations, each tagged with its own required time complexity, that is the signal this is a design problem. Your first move should be to write down every operation and its target complexity before thinking about any specific structure.

content.title: 2. The Core Skill: Combining Structures to Satisfy Multiple Constraints

blocks.text: Every structure you have studied trades one property for another. Arrays give O(1) indexed access but O(n) arbitrary removal. Hash maps give O(1) lookup but no ordering. Linked lists give O(1) insertion and removal at a known node but no O(1) indexed access. Heaps give O(log n) access to an extreme value but no efficient access to arbitrary elements.

Design problems are built so that no single one of these trades is good enough on its own. The way through is to pair a structure that is strong exactly where another is weak, so that the combination has no remaining weak spot.

items: A hash map is weak at ordering; a doubly linked list is strong at reordering in O(1). Paired together, you get O(1) lookup and O(1) reordering.
An array is weak at O(1) removal from the middle; swapping the target element with the last element before popping turns that removal into O(1).
A single heap only tracks one extreme value at a time; using two heaps, one for each half of the data, gives you O(log n) access to the middle.
A plain stack has no memory of past minimums once they are popped; a second, auxiliary stack that tracks the running minimum alongside the main one restores O(1) access to it.

blocks.text: This is why the pattern group is called Data Structure Design rather than, say, Hash Maps or Heaps. It draws directly on everything you already know about arrays, hash maps, linked lists, stacks, and heaps, and asks you to synthesize them instead of applying any one of them in isolation.

Think of it as a capstone skill. Every earlier DSA topic taught you one tool in isolation. This one teaches you how to reach for the right pair, or trio, of tools when a single one is provably not enough.
Every design problem can be approached the same way, regardless of which specific operations it asks for.

items: Step 1: Write down every required operation and its target time complexity. Do not skip this, it is the actual specification of the problem.
Step 2: For each operation, list every structure you know that can perform it at that complexity, in isolation.
Step 3: Look for a structure that appears in every list from step 2. If one exists, you are done, a single structure is enough.

Step 4: If no single structure appears in every list, which is the common case, look for a small set of structures that together cover every operation, and work out how they need to stay in sync with each other.
Step 5: Trace through the trickiest operation by hand on paper, usually the one with the tightest complexity requirement, and confirm every structure updates correctly for it.

blocks.text: Step 4 is where a small toolkit of recurring combinations becomes useful. A handful of structure pairings reappear across almost every design problem asked in interviews, so recognizing them by name saves you from rediscovering them from scratch under time pressure.

blocks.caption: Work backward from the required operations to the structure combination that satisfies all of them
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762093-321861062.png

content.title: 4. The Recurring Toolkit at a Glance

blocks.text: The following five combinations cover the overwhelming majority of design problems asked in interviews. Learn the shape of each one and you will recognize which to reach for within the first minute of reading a new problem.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Requirement","Structures Combined","Classic Problem"],"rows":[["O(1) lookup by key and O(1) reordering","Hash map + doubly linked list","LRU Cache"],["O(1) insert, O(1) delete by value, O(1) uniform random pick","Hash map + array with swap and pop","Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)"],["O(log n) insert, O(1) access to the running median","Max heap + min heap","Find Median from Data Stream"],["O(1) push, pop, and running minimum","Main stack + auxiliary stack","Min Stack"],["O(1) amortized running maximum over a sliding window","Sliding window + monotonic deque","Sliding Window Maximum"]]}

blocks.text: The next five sections walk through each of these combinations one at a time, explaining why the single structure fails and exactly how the pairing fixes it.

content.title: 5. Hash Map + Doubly Linked List for O(1) Access and O(1) Reordering

blocks.text: This combination shows up whenever a problem needs O(1) lookup by key and O(1) reordering based on usage, most famously in LRU Cache.

A hash map alone gives O(1) lookup, but it has no concept of order, so it cannot tell you which key was used least recently. A linked list alone can maintain order and move a node to the front in O(1) once you have a pointer to it, but finding that node by key in the first place would take O(n) without help.

The fix is to store the actual list nodes as the hash map values. The hash map maps each key directly to its node pointer, so lookup is O(1). The doubly linked list keeps every node ordered by recency, most recently used near the head, least recently used near the tail, so reordering is O(1) once you already hold the pointer.

items: A doubly linked list is required, not a singly linked one. Unlinking a node from the middle in O(1) needs both its previous and next pointers; a singly linked list only gives you next, so removing an arbitrary node would force an O(n) scan to find its predecessor.
Moving a node to the front on every access is what encodes recency. No separate timestamp or counter is needed, position in the list is the recency signal.

blocks.caption: LRU Cache: a hash map gives O(1) lookup, a doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762093-282199514.png
blocks.alt: Hash Map + Doubly Linked List for O1 Access and O1 Reordering

blocks.text: This exact combination is the single most tested design pairing in interviews. If you internalize nothing else from this topic, internalize this one.

content.title: 6. Hash Map + Array with Swap and Pop for O(1) Removal

blocks.text: This combination shows up whenever a problem needs O(1) insert, O(1) delete by an arbitrary value, and O(1) uniform random access, the exact requirements of Insert Delete GetRandom O(1).

A dynamic array gives O(1) insert at the end and O(1) indexed access, which makes uniform random selection trivial: pick a random index. But deleting an arbitrary value normally means finding it, then shifting every element after it, an O(n) operation.

The fix is the swap and pop trick, combined with a hash map that maps each value to its current index in the array. To remove a value, look up its index in O(1), swap that element with the last element of the array, update the hash map entry for the element that just moved, then pop the last element off the back. No shifting is required.

items: The array is never kept sorted or ordered in any meaningful way, which is exactly why it is safe to move elements around freely during removal.
The hash map exists purely to translate a value into an array index in O(1); the array itself is what makes random access and the swap possible.

blocks.caption: The swap and pop trick turns an O(n) middle removal into an O(1) removal
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762093-611068430.png
blocks.alt: Hash Map + Array with Swap and Pop for O1 Removal

blocks.text: The key realization is that this problem never asks for insertion order to be preserved. Whenever order does not matter, swap and pop is available; the moment a problem asks you to preserve order, this trick is off the table.

content.title: 7. Two Heaps for a Running Median

blocks.text: This combination shows up whenever a problem needs to maintain the median of a growing stream of numbers, with new numbers arriving one at a time, the requirement behind Find Median from Data Stream.

A single sorted array would let you read the median in O(1), but inserting a new number into sorted position costs O(n). A single heap gives O(log n) access to only one extreme, the minimum or the maximum, never the middle.

The fix is to split the data across two heaps. A max heap holds the smaller half of the numbers seen so far, and a min heap holds the larger half. Both heaps are kept balanced so their sizes never differ by more than one element. The median is then either the top of whichever heap is larger, or the average of both tops when the sizes are equal.

items: Insertion costs O(log n) because it pushes into a heap and may trigger one rebalancing move, itself a constant number of heap operations.
Reading the median costs O(1) because it only ever looks at the top of one or both heaps, never traverses either one.

blocks.caption: Two heaps split the stream in half so the median is always at the top
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406762093-250907252.png
blocks.alt: Two Heaps for a Running Median

content.title: 8. Auxiliary Stack for O(1) Running Minimum or Maximum

blocks.text: This combination shows up whenever a stack needs to report its current minimum, or maximum, in O(1) at every point in time, the requirement behind Min Stack.

A plain stack has no memory of past values once something is pushed on top of them. If the current minimum gets popped, recovering the new minimum would mean scanning whatever remains on the stack, an O(n) operation.

The fix is a second, auxiliary stack that tracks the running minimum alongside the main one. Push onto the auxiliary stack whenever the incoming value is less than or equal to its current top. Pop from the auxiliary stack whenever the value being popped from the main stack equals its top. The auxiliary stack top is always the current minimum.

items: Pushing an equal value onto the auxiliary stack, not just a strictly smaller one, is what makes popping duplicates of the current minimum correct.
The same idea extends directly to a running maximum by flipping the comparison, and to two auxiliary stacks at once if a problem needs both min and max simultaneously.

content.title: 9. Sliding Window + Deque for a Running Maximum

blocks.text: This combination shows up whenever a fixed size window slides across an array and the problem asks for the maximum inside the window at every position, the requirement behind Sliding Window Maximum.
Recomputing the maximum from scratch at every window position costs O(n times k). A plain queue of the window elements cannot discard values that have become irrelevant without an O(k) scan.

The fix is a deque of indices, kept so that the values they point to are always in decreasing order from front to back. Before adding a new index, pop from the back every index whose value is smaller than the incoming one, since those values can never be the maximum again while the new, larger value is in the window. Pop from the front whenever the front index has slid outside the window.

items: The front of the deque is always the index of the current window maximum, giving O(1) reads.
Each index is pushed and popped from the deque at most once across the whole array, giving O(n) total work, or O(1) amortized per step.

content.title: 10. Worked Example: LRU Cache From Scratch

blocks.text: The requirements are: get(key) in O(1), returning the value or -1 if the key is absent, and put(key, value) in O(1), inserting or updating a key and evicting the least recently used key whenever capacity is exceeded.

The design decision follows directly from the toolkit above: a hash map from key to node pointer for O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list of those same nodes ordered by recency. Two dummy sentinel nodes, a head and a tail, sit at the ends of the list so that inserting or removing at either end never needs a null check.
Why hash map plus doubly linked list

The hash map turns get and put from an O(n) search into an O(1) lookup of the node pointer. The doubly linked list turns reordering that node into O(1) work, because removeNode and insertAtFront only ever touch a fixed number of pointers, never traverse the list.
Walking through get(key)

If the key is missing, return -1 immediately. Otherwise, fetch the node in O(1) through the hash map, move it to the front of the list to mark it as most recently used, and return its value. Every access, even a read, changes the recency order.
Walking through put(key, value)

If the key already exists, update its value in place and move its node to the front, exactly like a successful get. If the key is new and the cache is already at capacity, evict the node just before the tail sentinel, which is always the least recently used node, remove it from both the list and the hash map, then insert the new node at the front.
Why the complexity is O(1)

Every operation the code performs, a hash map lookup, a pointer relink at the front of the list, or a pointer relink at the tail, is a fixed number of steps that does not grow with the number of keys stored. That is what makes both get and put true O(1), not just amortized or average case.

content.title: 11. Worked Example: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)

blocks.text: The requirements are: insert(val) in O(1), returning whether the value was newly added, remove(val) in O(1), returning whether the value was present, and getRandom() in O(1), returning a uniformly random element currently stored.

The design decision follows the toolkit combination above: a dynamic array, vector<int>, holding the actual values for O(1) indexed access, paired with a hash map from value to its current index in that array, enabling the swap and pop removal trick.
Walking through insert and remove

insert checks the hash map in O(1) to reject duplicates, then appends to the back of the vector and records its index, both O(1). remove looks up the index of the target value, overwrites it with whatever value currently sits at the back of the vector, fixes that moved value entry in the hash map, then pops the back of the vector, all O(1) and none of it requires shifting any other element.
Why getRandom stays uniform

Because values is a plain contiguous array with no gaps, ever, picking a uniformly random index and reading it in O(1) is guaranteed to pick each stored value with equal probability. This only holds because removal never leaves a hole, the swap and pop trick fills every hole immediately.
Every operation runs in O(1): a hash map lookup or insert, one array append or overwrite, and one random index draw. None of them scale with the number of elements stored.
Once the five core combinations are familiar, most other design problems turn out to be direct extensions or mashups of them.

items: Min Stack: a main stack plus an auxiliary stack tracking the running minimum, covered in the toolkit above.

LFU Cache: an extension of LRU Cache that evicts the least frequently used key instead of the least recently used one. It is typically built with a hash map from key to node, a hash map from frequency to a doubly linked list of keys at that frequency, and a pointer tracking the current minimum frequency.

Design Twitter: a hash map from user to their posted tweet ids with timestamps, a hash map from user to the set of users they follow, and a merge across followees timelines to produce the most recent tweets.
Find Median from Data Stream: the two heap combination covered above, one max heap for the lower half and one min heap for the upper half.

All O(1) Data Structure: a hash map from key to its count plus a doubly linked list of buckets ordered by count, where each bucket holds the set of keys sharing that count, giving O(1) increment, decrement, and access to the current maximum and minimum key.

blocks.text: Each variation is still the same underlying skill: list the operations and their target complexities, then find, or extend, a combination of structures that covers every single one.
A representative set of design problems you are likely to encounter, roughly in order of how often they appear.

items: Medium LRU Cache (LC 146): the canonical hash map plus doubly linked list design problem
Hard LFU Cache (LC 460): hash map plus frequency buckets built from doubly linked lists
Medium Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) (LC 380): hash map plus array with the swap and pop trick
Medium Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) with Duplicates Allowed (LC 381): the same combo extended to a multiset of indices
Easy Min Stack (LC 155): main stack plus an auxiliary minimum tracking stack
Hard Find Median from Data Stream (LC 295): two heaps balancing the lower and upper halves of the stream
Medium Design Twitter (LC 355): hash maps for tweets and follows combined with a merge across followees
Hard All O(1) Data Structure (LC 432): hash map plus a doubly linked list of frequency buckets
Medium Sliding Window Maximum (LC 239): a monotonic deque of indices maintaining a running maximum
Medium Design Circular Queue (LC 622): array plus head and tail indices with modular arithmetic

blocks.text: Most bugs in design problems come from the seams between structures, not from any single structure itself.

items: Updating one structure but forgetting to update its partner in the same operation, for example moving a node in the linked list on get but forgetting the hash map still points at a valid node.
Picking a structure that satisfies most, but not all, of the required operations, then discovering during coding that the last operation cannot hit its target complexity.
Not handling the eviction and capacity edge case in cache style problems, for example forgetting to erase the evicted key from the hash map, which leaves a dangling pointer bug.
Using a singly linked list where a doubly linked list is required. Without a previous pointer, you cannot unlink an arbitrary node in O(1).
Forgetting that the swap and pop trick changes the order of elements. It is only safe when the problem never needs to preserve order.
Letting the two heaps in a running median solution drift apart in size instead of rebalancing them after every insert, which silently breaks the O(1) median read.
Have you written down every required operation and its target time complexity before choosing a structure?
Can you name, for each operation, which structures support it at that complexity in isolation?
Have you identified which combination of hash map, array, heap, stack, or linked list covers every operation together?
Can you implement the LRU Cache hash map plus doubly linked list combo from scratch in under ten minutes?
Can you implement the swap and pop removal trick used in Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)?
Have you handled the capacity and eviction edge case if the problem involves a cache?
Do your auxiliary structures, a second stack, a second heap, frequency buckets, stay perfectly in sync with the main structure on every mutation?

blocks.text: If you can answer every one of these without hesitation, you are ready for any design problem an interviewer can throw at you, because the skill being tested is always the same: turn a list of constraints into the smallest combination of familiar structures that satisfies all of them at once.
